rv.q: This is a heartwarming, refreshing and original show, flamboyantly stirred by director Roy Alexander Weise, in which simmering emotions come fiercely to the boil.
Though overlong, this is a tasty, stimulating experience.
Weise’s production savours both the playfulness and the emotional truths in the plot, and his cast all give affectionately observed and beautifully rounded performances.
Half way through Roy Alexander Weise’s delightfully acted, ebullient production of Katori Hall’s Pulitzer Prize winner, the scent of spiced chicken wings wafts through the auditorium...
Like smashing a plate of hot ones, Hall’s play is a pleasure, but there are moments where it feels like an endurance test.

This far more unifying second act grabs you with spicy intrigue around the competition and emotional reckonings between the central lovers as well as Dwayne’s nephew, Everett (Kaireece Denton), and his father (Dwayne Walcott), whose story rises to the fore.
But the play’s achingly slow pace and contrived conversations keep the drama from generating the compelling heat that it should.
It’s a pity that the skeletal plot keeps veering into soap-style homilies, because Hall is addressing some weighty themes.
Katori Hall’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play makes the mouth water and the heart ache.
Hall's flavours may not always mix and the bombastic jauntiness makes the melodramatic moments feel drawn out by contrast, but so what. This is a summer comfort watch.
Most of the nearly three-hour performance time is fast, playful banter with the serious elements mostly emerging just before the interval.
This is a genial play but the balance between the more serious 'soap opera' style scenes and broad comedy does jar at times...
Thankfully, the sentimentality is tempered somewhat by some outrageous comedy.

Hall, a 2010. Olivier-winner for her Martin Luther King-themed The Mountaintop, rides the waves of brio for a while until such time as her overwritten comedy-drama turns in on itself well before the play has reached the (nearly) three-hour mark.
There's richness of writing here, and the sheer enjoyment evident from the ensemble cast carries it resoundingly.

This shapeless, facile drama isn’t really a show but a cookery demonstration hosted by a quartet of witless buffoons trying to be funny and occasionally breaking character to perform karaoke routines.

cn.t: Hall's Pulitzer-winner earns praise for its rare portrayal of queer Black men and warm performances, but critics find the 165-minute runtime overstuffed, with tonal shifts between comedy and drama not fully landing.
